title: Delete with an ownership check
idea: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. Delete checks that the URL's `user_id` is the caller's.
points: Look the row up first. No row means `404`.
A row owned by someone else gets `403`: known caller, not allowed.
Only the owner's request reaches `delete`, which replies `204` with no body.
`req.params.id` is text. Convert it with `Number()` and reject bad ids with `404`.

steps.caption: `requireAuth` verifies the token and sets `req.user` to Ada, user 1.
The lookup finds URL 1, so the request goes on.
URL 1 has `user_id` 1, the same as Ada. The check passes.
Only now does the route delete the row.
Grace sends `DELETE /codes/2`. Her token is valid and the URL exists, so she reaches the owner check.
URL 2 has `user_id` 1, not 2. The route replies `403` and deletes nothing.
Ada sends `DELETE /codes/99`. Her token is valid, so the lookup runs.
No row has id 99, so there is no owner to check. The route replies `404`.

code.title: DELETE /codes/:id
code.caption: The service decides; the controller maps its answer to a status. The calls at the end cover every branch.

walk.text: Find the row first. Only its `user_id` is needed.
No row gives `not_found`, which the controller turns into `404`.
Another owner means `forbidden`. Both ids are numbers, so `!==` compares correctly.
Only the owner gets this far: delete the row.
Convert the id and reject anything that is not a valid `serial` id as `404`.
Map each answer to a status: `404`, `403` or `204` with no body.
`401` without a token, `403` for a stranger, `204` for the owner, then `404` three ways.

pitfalls: Never delete by `id` alone. Check the owner first, or any user can delete any URL.
`sub` is a string. Convert it with `Number`, or every owner looks like a stranger.

quiz.q: Ada (user 1) owns URL 1. URL 9 does not exist. What prints?
quiz.why: User 2 does not own URL 1: `forbidden`. URL 9 has no row: `not_found`. User 1 owns URL 1, so it is `deleted`.

takeaway: Look up the row, compare its owner to the caller, then delete.

starters: Why 403 and not 404 for someone else's URL?
What if two requests delete the same URL at once?
Should deleting be a soft delete instead?
